passages.t: A funeral song, and a call to seek and live
passages.happening:
Amos takes up a funeral song over Israel. ‘Fallen is Virgin Israel, never to rise again’ (verse 2), lying abandoned on her land with no one to lift her up. A town that marches out a thousand strong will see a hundred come back, and one that marches out a hundred will have ten left (verse 3).

Yet the LORD still calls. ‘Seek Me and live’ is his word to the house of Israel (verse 4). They are not to seek Bethel or go to Gilgal or travel down to Beersheba, for Gilgal will go into exile and Bethel will come to nothing (verse 5). ‘Seek the LORD and live’ (verse 6), or he will sweep like fire through the house of Joseph, with no one at Bethel to put it out.
passages.hearers:
A lament was a funeral song, sung with a limping rhythm, usually for someone already dead. Amos spoke around 760 BC, when the north under Jeroboam II was at its height, so a funeral song for the nation would have sounded absurd to his hearers. Yet within four decades Assyria had destroyed Samaria. Verse 3 describes the losses of a militia raised from towns and villages.

Bethel and Gilgal were the north's main shrines. Beersheba, in the far south of Judah, was tied to Abraham and Isaac, and northerners evidently went there on pilgrimage across the border. Amos sets the shrines against God himself. People were seeking holy places instead of the Holy One.

The call to seek and live holds the door open even in a funeral song. Many scholars see the first seventeen verses of the chapter built in a mirror pattern around a center: lament at the start and wailing at the end, calls to seek and live, charges of corrupted justice, and in the middle a hymn to God the creator.
passages.later: Abraham called on the LORD at Beersheba (Genesis 21:33), and Isaac built an altar there (Genesis 26:23-25). Isaiah gives the same call: ‘Seek the LORD while He may be found’ (Isaiah 55:6).
passages.asks: God calls Israel to seek him, not his shrines. Ask whether you have been seeking places, practices or experiences more than God himself. And ask what it would mean for you this week to seek the LORD and live.

passages.t: Justice turned to wormwood, and justice in the gate
passages.happening:
‘There are those who turn justice into wormwood and cast righteousness to the ground’ (verse 7). Against them stands the one who made the Pleiades and Orion, who turns darkness into dawn and pours the sea over the earth: ‘the LORD is His name’ (verse 8).

They hate the one who speaks up in the gate and despise anyone who speaks with integrity (verse 10). Because they trample the poor and take grain from them, they will never live in the stone houses they have built or drink the wine of their vineyards (verse 11). They take bribes and deprive the poor of justice in the gate (verse 12), and the prudent keep silent, for the days are evil (verse 13).

‘Seek good, not evil, so that you may live’ (verse 14). ‘Hate evil and love good; establish justice in the gate. Perhaps the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph’ (verse 15). Otherwise there will be wailing in every square and every vineyard when the LORD passes through (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
In an Israelite town the city gate was the public square and the courtroom. Elders sat in its passageway to hear disputes and witness agreements. When Amos says the powerful hate the one who reproves in the gate and deprive the poor of justice there, he means the village court, where an ordinary person could get a fair hearing, has been bought.

Wormwood was a plant known for its bitter taste. To turn justice into wormwood is to make what should heal into something poisonous. The stone houses were built of hewn, squared stone, an expensive kind of building found in royal and wealthy houses at Samaria in this period. The tax of grain was probably rents or levies taken from small farmers.

The hymn of verses 8 and 9 sits at the center of the chapter's pattern. The Pleiades and Orion are the star cluster and constellation still known by those names. The God who set the stars in place is the judge of the court that has been bought. And yet verse 15 leaves a door open: perhaps the LORD will be gracious to a remnant.
passages.later: The law sent cases to the elders at the city gate (Deuteronomy 21:19), and Boaz settled Ruth's case there (Ruth 4:1-11). Job also praises God as ‘the Maker of the Bear and Orion, of the Pleiades’ (Job 9:9).
passages.asks: The powerful hated anyone who spoke up for the truth in court. Ask whether you have resented someone who told you the truth. And verse 15 asks for more than avoiding evil. Ask where you could help establish justice in your own gate, your workplace, your church or your town.

passages.t: The Day of darkness, and let justice roll
passages.happening:
“Woe to you who long for the Day of the LORD!” (verse 18). It will be darkness and not light. It will be like a man who runs from a lion and meets a bear, or goes into his house, leans on the wall and is bitten by a snake (verse 19).

Then God speaks of Israel's worship. He hates and despises their feasts and cannot stand their solemn assemblies (verse 21). He will not accept their burnt offerings, grain offerings or peace offerings (verse 22). He will not listen to their songs and harps (verse 23). ‘But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream’ (verse 24).

‘Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?’ (verse 25). They have carried along Sakkuth and Kaiwan, idols they made (verse 26), and so God will send them into exile beyond Damascus (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The Day of the LORD was already a popular hope in Israel, a day when God would fight for his people against their enemies. Amos turns it around. For a people living in injustice, the Day will be darkness. The pictures in verse 19 are of a danger escaped only to meet a worse one, and of being struck in the place one thought was safe.

Verse 24 has echoed through history as a call for faith to show itself in public justice. Justice is fair judgment in court and fair dealing in the market. Righteousness is right relationships kept. A stream that runs all year, in a land where most streams dry up in summer, is the picture of justice that does not stop.

Sakkuth and Kaiwan are generally taken as names or titles of Mesopotamian star gods, Kaiwan linked with the planet Saturn, though their exact identity and the Hebrew of the verse are debated. Beyond Damascus means into Assyrian territory in Mesopotamia and beyond, where Israel was deported after Samaria fell.

Readers across the political spectrum have claimed Amos. The book itself speaks to God's people and their leaders, and its standard is God's covenant, not any modern program.
passages.later: Stephen quoted verses 25 to 27, following the Greek translation, to show Israel's long history of idolatry: ‘Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?’ (Acts 7:42). Micah asks what the LORD requires, and answers, ‘to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God’ (Micah 6:8).
passages.hard:
Does Amos reject sacrifice and worship altogether?

Verses 21 to 25 sound as if God rejects Israel's whole system of worship, and verse 25 asks whether Israel brought sacrifices in the wilderness. Some scholars have concluded that Amos opposed sacrifice in principle, or knew a tradition in which sacrifice played little part in the wilderness years. Most interpreters read the passage differently. Amos speaks to a particular people whose worship went on beside bribery and oppression, and similar words in other prophets reject worship without obedience, not worship as such. On this reading, verse 25 points out that Israel's relationship with God in the wilderness rested on more than offerings, or that even then Israel mixed its worship with idols (verse 26).

What the passage makes unmistakable is that God does not accept worship as a substitute for justice. The debate is about how far the rejection reaches, not about that central point.
passages.asks: God would rather have justice than music. Ask whether your worship and your treatment of people belong to the same life. And ask whether you have longed for God's day as a day against others, when it may be a day that searches you first.
